videos.description:
Six days after a Learjet 60 fell 35,000 feet over Palm Beach County, investigators have pumped the crater dry and pulled out part of an engine. Pieces of the tail turned up almost four miles away. And a recording has resurfaced: six months earlier, the same jet couldn't hold its altitude in severe turbulence. ✈️

This is Part 2 of our reconstruction of N722BD, the Learjet that crashed on Military Trail on November 1st, 2026, killing all nine people on board. Everything here is on the record: the real air traffic control recordings, the NTSB's statements, news reports, and the raw ADS-B tracking data, which we analysed ourselves. In that data, the "eight-second level-off" many people quote looks like a frozen altitude reading.

We go through five updates: the co-pilot's text message and her father's answer to the online criticism, the tail pieces and the debris on nearby roofs, the eight seconds that never happened, the crater dig and the missing cockpit voice recorder, and the same jet in May. Then the theories, from the missile rumours to the storm, and what the evidence says about each.

No cause has been determined. This is a reconstruction. Where something is our own analysis, we say so.

Our thoughts are with the families of captain Jeff Gregory, co-pilot Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras, Adam Robinson, Helen Sharp, their children Emma and Charlie, Ana María Ramírez Cetina, Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr.

videos.title: The Last 8 Seconds Before Two Helicopters Collided Near Everest
videos.description:
Eight seconds. That's how long the helipad camera at Pheriche, near Mount Everest, shows the first helicopter before two of them meet over the same patch of snow. 🚁 On Tuesday morning, 3 November 2026, a red Fishtail Air AS350 coming down from Gorak Shep and a white Air Dynasty AS350 on a cargo flight from Lukla came in to land at the same helipad, more than 4,000 metres up. A line of trekkers was waiting a few steps away.

In this animated reconstruction, we go through the real helipad footage frame by frame and rebuild those eight seconds in 3D: who came from where, which helicopter was descending faster, where the rotor struck, and why there was no controller to separate them. Then we look at why the sky over Nepal is one of the hardest places in the world to fly, through three other cases: Lukla 2019, Kathmandu 2018 with the real tower recording, and Pokhara 2023.

How do two helicopters end up over the same spot in clear weather, on a pad big enough for seven? What did investigators recommend after an earlier crash in the same valley? And what is still unanswered?

No cause has been determined. This is a reconstruction based on the real footage, official statements and news reports. Where sources disagree, we say so.

Our thoughts are with the family and friends of Vasanth Kumar Balaramudu, 47, from Chennai, India, who was killed, and with everyone injured.

What can a jet's tracking data tell us about those final 77 seconds? Why is the weather a major focus for investigators? And what does it mean that the aircraft may have been breaking up before impact?

No cockpit recording has been released and no cause has been determined. Where sources disagree, we say so. The NTSB's preliminary report is expected in about 30 days; the final report can take a year or two.

Our thoughts are with the families and friends of the nine people on board: captain Jeff Gregory, co-pilot Nathalia Filgueiras, Adam Robinson, Helen Sharp, their two children, Rachael Reed, Charmi Fehr and Ana María Ramírez Cetina.

videos.title: If You Woke Up Buried Alive, This Was Your Escape Plan
videos.description:
For a long time, one of the most terrifying questions around death was surprisingly simple:

What if the doctor was wrong?

During the nineteenth century, fear of premature burial inspired inventors to design coffins with bells, ladders, spring-loaded lids, flags, air tubes, mechanical fans and even electrical alarm systems connecting graves to a central station.

These were not just horror-story concepts.

They were patented.

This episode follows the real history of “safety coffins”: from Christian Henry Eisenbrandt's 1843 life-preserving coffin, to Franz Vester's ladder-and-bell system, Albert Fearnaught's grave signal, increasingly elaborate mechanical caskets, and an 1887 design that imagined an entire cemetery wired like an alarm network.

But the strangest part comes at the end.

For all the patents, bells and escape systems, there is no reliable documented rescue we can point to from one of these patented safety coffins.

The machines tell us less about how often people were actually buried alive and much more about how uncertain death once felt.

If you enjoyed this story, leave a like, tell us what we should uncover next, and subscribe to TALEYE — look closer.

videos.title: Why Was He Cutting Their Hair While They Slept?
videos.description:
In 1942, while the United States was at war, a series of unsettling nighttime intrusions terrified Pascagoula, Mississippi.

People woke up to discover that someone had entered their bedrooms while they slept and cut off pieces of their hair.

The newspapers gave the intruder a name: the Phantom Barber.

But the case quickly became stranger. What began as quiet bedroom break-ins eventually became linked to a violent assault, a townwide panic, wartime blackout conditions, Pinkerton involvement, and a suspect named William A. Dolan.

This episode follows the real events behind the Phantom Barber story: what happened, what was proven, what was never proven, and why the case still feels disturbing more than eighty years later.

videos.title: If This Black Car Stopped Beside You, You Were Told to Run
videos.description:
In 1970s Poland, children were warned about a black car.

A Volga.

Depending on who told the story, the people inside were priests, nuns, criminals, members of the secret police or something even stranger. Some versions claimed children were being kidnapped for their blood. Others said organs were being taken. Later versions abandoned the Volga completely, but kept the same warning: if a dark car stopped beside you, do not get close.

The disturbing part is that one piece of the story was real.

On April 3, 1965, three-year-old Lilianna Hencel was kidnapped in Warsaw. A witness reported seeing the two women with the child get into a black Volga taxi. Lilianna was later found alive. The driver of the Volga never came forward, and investigators never established the vehicle's registration number.

This episode follows the Black Volga from a recorded Polish urban legend to the real Warsaw kidnapping that may have helped give the story its power. It looks at why the Volga itself carried such an intimidating image, how the rumor changed every time it was retold, and why the legend survived even after the original car disappeared from the road.

The question is not whether a nationwide Black Volga kidnapping network really existed. There is no evidence that it did.

The stranger question is how little reality a frightening story needs before people begin looking over their shoulder.

If you enjoyed this story, leave a like, tell us what we should uncover next, and subscribe to TALEYE - look closer.

videos.title: This Cat Breed Exists Because of One Genetic Mutation
videos.description:
The Scottish Fold looks almost designed, round face, huge eyes, and ears folded so neatly forward that they completely change the cat’s expression.

But nobody designed those ears.

In 1961, a white farm cat named Susie was noticed near Coupar Angus in Scotland. Her unusual ears came from a naturally occurring mutation. Breeders liked the look, preserved it, crossed her descendants with other cats, and eventually turned one genetic accident into an internationally recognized breed.

But selective breeding preserved more than an appearance.

The same genetic variant associated with the Fold’s signature ears affects cartilage and bone — connecting the breed’s defining feature to Scottish Fold osteochondrodysplasia and a welfare debate that is still evolving today.

This episode follows the Scottish Fold from Susie and Snooks to TRPV4, Fold-to-Fold breeding, modern genetic testing, veterinary research and the licensing restrictions now applied to Scottish Fold breeding in Scotland.

And the science is more complicated than either side’s simplest version: two-copy cats have historically been associated with more severe disease, while one-copy cats can show very different outcomes.

Which leaves a much harder question:

Can we preserve the feature that defines a breed when the biology behind that feature is also the source of its controversy?

If you enjoyed this story, leave a like, tell us what we should uncover next, and subscribe to TALEYE — look closer.

videos.title: This Dog Breed Exists Because One Man Refused to Let It Die
videos.description:
The Cavalier King Charles Spaniel looks ancient almost timeless.

But the modern breed is surprisingly recent.

By the early 1900s, the long-faced toy spaniels seen in old royal paintings had nearly disappeared from the show world. Then an American named Roswell Eldridge offered British breeders money to bring that older type back.

What followed was one of the strangest breed-revival stories in dog history: old paintings became visual references, a dog named Ann’s Son became a living model, and breeders deliberately rebuilt a type that fashion had almost erased.

But selective breeding does more than change appearance.

Modern Cavaliers are also closely monitored for inherited health problems including mitral valve disease and syringomyelia raising a much bigger question about what happens when humans shape an animal generation after generation.

This episode follows the Cavalier from royal portraits to Crufts, from Ann’s Son to modern genetic screening, and asks a simple question:

Can we keep the dog we brought back and make its future healthier than its past?

If you enjoyed this story, leave a like, tell us what we should uncover next, and subscribe to TALEYE - look closer.

videos.description:
Some of the fruit sitting in a supermarket today did not exist in its modern form until humans made it possible.

So can humans actually invent a fruit?

In this episode, we follow four increasingly strange examples: the modern strawberry, born from strawberry lineages brought together across continents; the seedless watermelon, produced through deliberately manipulated chromosome combinations; Cotton Candy grapes, selected through years of breeding for an unusual flavor; and a genetically engineered pineapple whose flesh grows pink.

The deeper you go, the harder it becomes to draw a clean line between "growing" a fruit and inventing one.

videos.title: What Happens to Your Data After You Press Send?
videos.description:
The internet feels wireless. But between continents, almost all of it travels through physical cables lying on the ocean floor.

This is the story of how engineers learned to connect continents beneath the sea — from the first nineteenth-century telegraph experiments to the fiber-optic systems that now carry more than 99% of international data.

We follow the failures of the first Atlantic cables, the Great Eastern, the birth of transatlantic telephony, fiber optics, modern cable-laying and repair ships, redundancy, and the new systems being planned for the AI era.

videos.title: Two loops, one fingertip #FingerprintPatterns #CompositeWhorl
videos.description:
The double-loop whorl is one of the more elaborate, rarer prints a finger can carry — two separate loop formations interlocking on one fingertip, each with its own center, bracketed by two deltas, like a yin-yang in skin. It belongs to the whorl family (genetics mapped via ADAMTS9-AS2 and the limb-development loci in Li et al., 2022, Cell), and forms when growth forces on the volar pad pull in two directions at once, so the ridges organize around two focal points instead of one. If your fingertip carries one, it’s a record of a busier moment in your own development.

videos.title: Whorls, Leukemia, and What Fingerprints Actually Tell Us #genetics #health
videos.description:
Plain whorl fingerprints — concentric bullseyes ringed by two deltas — are the second most common pattern after loops, and run noticeably higher in some East Asian populations (a population-level average, with wide individual variation). Whorls carry the firmest genetic signal of any print: a 2016 Journal of Investigative Dermatology study (Ho et al.) tied them to the gene ADAMTS9-AS2, and 2022 Cell research linked them, via EVI1, to slightly longer little fingers. Some studies have also noted whorls turning up more often among leukemia patients — an observed association in specific studies, not a prediction and not a proven cause. A whorl is a clue, never a verdict.

videos.title: Your fingerprints were grown, not stamped #science #mindblown
videos.description:
The tented arch is one of the rarest fingerprints a hand can carry — a plain arch with a sharp spike thrust up through the center, often with a tiny forming delta at its base. It sits on the knife-edge between an arch and a loop: nudge it a little either way and the whole category changes. Whether you get a flat arch or a spiked one comes down to how high the volar pad stood in the womb — a difference of fractions of a millimeter and a few days of timing, set by the same limb-development genetics mapped in Li et al. (2022), Cell. It’s living proof your fingerprints are grown, not stamped.

Why Plain Arch Fingerprints Are The Most Minimalist #FingerprintDesign #Dermatoglyphics
videos.description:
Plain arch fingerprints are the rarest of the three great pattern families — often just a few percent of fingers, though the figure swings widely by population through ordinary genetic drift. An arch has no looping core and no delta (the little triangle other patterns carry); the ridges simply stream across the fingertip. It forms when the volar pad has already flattened to almost nothing before the ridges set, leaving the same limb-development genes (mapped in Li et al., 2022, Cell) nothing to wrap around. It’s the minimalist’s fingerprint: the oldest, simplest way ridges can cross a fingertip.

videos.title: The Thumb-Ward Ridges Only 5% Have #fingerprints #rare
videos.description:
Radial loop fingerprints are the rarer mirror of the common loop — their ridges curl toward the thumb instead of the little finger, and they cluster on the index fingers. Like all loops, the pattern is set in the womb by the limb-development genetics (EVI1 and related loci) mapped in a 2022 Cell study (Li et al.), as the volar pad on the fingertip regresses just slightly unevenly. That small asymmetry in timing tips the whole ridge field thumb-ward. A radial loop is a quiet signature of how individual your own developmental clock was.

videos.title: Your Fingerprints Were Decided in the Womb #science #shorts
videos.description:
Ulnar loop fingerprints — the single most common pattern in the world — are shaped not by skin genes but by limb-development genes like EVI1. The ridges sweep toward the little finger, and that direction is locked in before birth, when volar pads on the fingertip regress in the womb. A 2022 study in Cell (Li et al.) found fingerprint patterns are drawn by the same genetic toolkit that builds your hands, with loops as the developmentally robust “middle path” most fingers settle into. Whatever else your hand is doing, odds are at least one finger carries an ulnar loop.

videos.description:
Tongue rolling — the famous 'dominant gene' myth: roughly 65 to 81 percent of people can curl the tongue into a tube, and for a century it was the number-one classroom example of Mendelian genetics. Alfred Sturtevant proposed a single dominant gene in 1940; in 1952 Philip Matlock found identical twins who differed, which a single gene makes impossible. Sturtevant himself called it embarrassing. Sources: Sturtevant (1940), Journal of Heredity; Matlock (1952).

Intermediate caffeine metabolizers are heterozygous at CYP1A2 rs762551 — one fast A copy, one slow C copy, the AC genotype — and they’re frequently the single largest group, around 41% to 45% of European and Asian samples. "Never goes bad." The little brown bottle on the barrel holds plain, unscented household bleach (sodium hypochlorite), counted out by the drop the way an old cistern family in Holmes County, Ohio still does it. The dose is the one the CDC and the EPA print on their emergency water sheets: 8 drops per gallon of 6% bleach, or 6 drops of 8.25%, stir, wait 30 minutes, faint pool smell. Drops are for jugs; for anything bigger use the CDC's teaspoon: about ⅛ teaspoon per gallon of 6% bleach, so a 55-gallon barrel takes about 7 teaspoons (2 tablespoons + 1 teaspoon) of 6%, or about 5 teaspoons (1 tablespoon + 2 teaspoons) of 8.25%: less than a dime's worth of bleach.

We answer the four questions everyone asks. Does it really keep water safe for years? Water itself does not go bad; care does. In a clean food-grade container, sealed, cool and dark, with a ten-minute check once a year it can sit for years (the official CDC rule is to replace home-filled water every six months: follow it if you want the book's rule, the drops are the same either way). What does it cost? A $2–4 jug, and the "water preserver" sold in emergency catalogs for $13–28 a bottle is the same chemical, sodium hypochlorite at 5.25%. What can it NOT do? It does not remove lead, fuel, pesticides or any chemical, it does not kill Cryptosporidium, and it does not make pond or creek water safe: it protects clean water, it does not clean dirty water. Is it safe to drink? It is the same chlorine already in city tap water, at the dose the agencies publish.

SAFETY: Use only plain, regular, UNSCENTED liquid household bleach (5–9% sodium hypochlorite). No scented, splashless, gel, pods or "cleaner with bleach". In this video, we break down the neuroscience of why dreams feel so convincing:
→ The Activation-Synthesis Hypothesis (Hobson & McCarley, 1977)
→ Why your visual cortex "sees" dreams the same way it sees reality
→ The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex — the switch your brain flips every night
→ Lucid dreaming and what it tells us about consciousness
→ Sleep paralysis: when the dream forgets to end

If you've ever woken up from a dream and thought "how did I not know that wasn't real?" — this video is your answer.

videos.title: Did Ancient Humans Have Heart Attacks?
videos.description:
In this video, we explore the remarkable evidence showing that heart disease has existed for thousands of years. From a 3,500-year-old Egyptian princess with severe arterial calcification to clogged arteries found in mummies from Peru, the American Southwest, and the Aleutian Islands, the story of cardiovascular disease stretches deep into our human past. Discover how ancient humans experienced atherosclerosis long before fast food or cigarettes, why scientists have found evidence of arterial plaques in mummies from cultures across the globe, and how researchers are using advanced CT scans to uncover the true history of heart disease.
Learn why heart attacks are not simply a product of modern civilization, why longer lifespans make them far more common today, and how ancient risk factors like indoor smoke, chronic infections, and parasites drove the very same disease process we see in hospitals today. Heart disease is not just a medical challenge of the modern world. It is one of the oldest threats ever faced by the human heart. And for the first time in that long history, humanity has the tools to understand it — and fight back.
Sources:
Armelagos, G. J., Brown, P. J., & Turner, B. (2005). Evolutionary, historical and political economic perspectives on health and disease. Social Science & Medicine, 61(4), 755–765.
Thompson, R. C., Allam, A. H., Lombardi, G. P., Wann, L. S., Sutherland, M. L., Sutherland, J. D., ... & Thomas, G. S. (2013). Atherosclerosis across 4000 years of human history: the HORUS study of four ancient populations. The Lancet, 381(9873), 1211–1222.
David, A. R., Zimmerman, M. R., & Aufderheide, A. C. (2010). Cancer: An old disease, a new disease or something in between? Nature Reviews Cancer, 10(10), 728–733.
Allam, A. H., Thompson, R. C., Wann, L. S., Miyamoto, M. I., & Thomas, G. S. (2009). Computed tomographic assessment of atherosclerosis in ancient Egyptian mummies. JAMA, 302(19), 2091–2094.

videos.title: How Did Ancient Humans Hunt Animals 10x Their Size?
videos.description:
Ancient humans hunted some of the largest animals in Earth’s history — without modern weapons, farming, or technology.

Yet they became the most successful hunters to ever exist.

From mammoth spear traps and gravity-based boulder ambushes to desert mega-traps, poisoned arrows, endurance hunting, and coordinated group strategies, prehistoric humans developed survival systems that were far more advanced than most people realize.

In this video, we break down the real science, archaeology, and evolutionary intelligence behind how humans hunted Ice Age megafauna like mammoths, gazelles, ibex, kudu, and other dangerous prey across prehistoric environments.

These hunting strategies combined:
physics, biology, chemistry, landscape engineering, animal psychology, teamwork, and early communication systems.

🧠 In this video, you’ll learn:

• Planted Spear Theory — How researchers suggest hunters used a charging mammoth’s own momentum as a weapon
• Boulder Ambush Hunting — How gravity and terrain were used instead of direct combat
• Desert Kites — Massive prehistoric trap systems found across the Middle East and Central Asia
• Poison Arrow Technology — 60,000-year-old chemical hunting systems discovered in Africa
• Persistence Hunting — How humans evolved as endurance predators capable of chasing animals to exhaustion
• Coordinated Group Hunts — How language and planning enabled large-scale hunting operations
• Human–Dog Hunting Alliance — The earliest known partnership between humans and wolves
• The Intelligence Advantage — How memory, learning, and cooperation made humans apex predators

For hundreds of thousands of years, survival wasn’t about strength — it was about intelligence, patience, coordination, and adaptation.

Ancient humans didn’t dominate because they were physically superior.

They dominated because they could think ahead, plan collectively, and learn faster than any other species.

Every piece of meat consumed today is the result of hundreds of thousands of years of survival innovation.

⚠️ DISCLAIMER

This video presents archaeological, anthropological, and scientific research for educational purposes. Some hunting methods are directly supported by evidence, while others are based on experimental archaeology, terrain analysis, and scientific interpretation. New discoveries may refine these theories over time.

• Paleoindian mammoth hunting studies
• Cave of Hearths projectile findings (South Africa)
• Desert Kite research (PNAS, Antiquity, 2022)
• Science Advances (2026) poison arrow residue analysis

• Human–dog hunting domestication studies

videos.title: Roman Emperors Ate This Rotten Fish Sauce Every Day

What did Julius Caesar actually eat?
The answer is far stranger than most people realize.

Ancient Romans — including emperors, senators, and soldiers — were obsessed with garum, a fermented fish sauce made from rotting fish guts left under the Mediterranean sun for months. It was poured over meat, bread, wine, and nearly every meal in the Roman world.

But that was only the beginning.

In this video, we explore:

The disgusting truth about Roman food
Why garum was the ketchup of Ancient Rome
The shocking process behind Roman fish sauce
Why Roman wine secretly contained lead
The bizarre luxury foods eaten by the Roman elite
How modern foods like Worcestershire sauce and fish sauce are surprisingly similar to garum
The strange reality of daily life in Ancient Rome

From liquefied fish entrails to lead-sweetened wine, the diet of Rome’s most powerful men was far more disturbing — and familiar — than you think.

videos.title: What Did Romans Do When They Got Sick
tags: what did romans do when they got sick
videos.description:
#RomanHistory #AncientRome #History

In ancient Rome, if you had epilepsy, your doctor had one cure 
— and it sent you to the colosseum. What Romans did when they 
got sick is one of the darkest, most overlooked stories in the 
history of medicine. And it didn't end when Rome fell.

In this video, we explore a medical practice documented by 
Rome's most respected physicians, practiced across the empire, 
and still recorded in use in the 1800s — nearly 2,000 years 
after it was first written down.

In this video, we discuss:

The Darkest Prescription: How Roman doctors used the colosseum 
floor as their pharmacy — and why the most powerful men in Rome 
believed it worked.

Pneuma — The Science of Vital Essence: The ancient medical 
theory that made gladiator blood a legitimate cure, not madness 
— and the name behind it that shaped 1,500 years of Western 
medicine.

After the Fall: How this practice survived the collapse of Rome, 
spread through medieval Europe, and was still documented in 
public squares in the 1800s.

The Quiet Truth: Why the cure appeared to work on some patients 
— and what that tells us about how humans have always understood 
medicine.

If you've ever assumed ancient medicine was just herbs and 
prayers, what Romans actually did when they got sick might be 
the most disturbing correction to that idea you'll ever hear.

Sources:

Gladiator blood as epilepsy cure (primary source): 
Celsus, A.C. De Medicina, Book III (c. 40 AD). 
"a miserable aid made tolerable by a malady still more miserable"

Pliny the Elder's account: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia 
(c. 77 AD). "The blood of gladiators is drunk by epileptics 
as though it were the draught of life"

Humoral theory and pneuma: Galen of Pergamon, 
On the Natural Faculties (c. 170 AD)

Modern historical research on the practice: 
Moog, F.P. & Karenberg, A. (2003). "Between Horror and Hope: 
Gladiator's Blood as a Cure for Epileptics in Ancient Medicine." 
Journal of the History of the Neurosciences, 12(2), 137–143.

Gladiatorial ban: Emperor Honorius, Imperial Edict (404 AD). 
Historical record.
